CalTopo's training and documentation site at training.caltopo.com is built on Grav, serving <meta name="generator" content="GravCMS" /> over Grav's learn2 documentation theme.

A page is a folder under user/pages/ containing a Markdown file. The file's Markdown/Frontmatter/Yaml carries title, slug, date, and publish state; its filename selects the Twig template; folder nesting is simultaneously the URL structure and the site navigation, with numeric folder prefixes setting order. Configuration is YAML under user/config/. Nothing is stored anywhere else — installing is unzipping an archive, with no schema and no install wizard.
What that buys: the entire site is git/Friendly plain text that diffs, branches, and edits in any editor, and backs up by copying a directory. The general shape of the tradeoff is on File/Flat.

What it costs: work a database would do with an index has to be recomputed instead, so Grav caches aggressively and its own requirements page recommends a PHP user cache — APCu, Memcached, or Redis — for acceptable performance. Relational content that a database gives away for free (multi-language, multi-user, cross-referenced collections) instead needed a purpose-built object layer, Flex, added in 2018.

Praised as “experimental and ethereal” and a “welcome addition to the new music scene,” the Hinge Quartet is made up of Philipp Stäudlin (saxophones), Dan VanHassel (electric guitar), Matt Sharrock (percussion), and Keith Kirchoff (piano). Lying somewhere between a chamber ensemble and an avant-garde rock band, the Hinge Quartet combines cutting-edge contemporary classical and experimental music with seamless multimedia integration and the innovative re-imagining of rock and pop songs.

Dedicated to expanding and diversifying the repertoire for their ensemble, the Hinge Quartet has commissioned new works from composers including Bahar Royaee, Per Bloland, Kirsten Volness, LJ White, Ed Martin, Chen-Hui Jen, Kirsten Carey, Marti Epstein, Yoon-Ji Lee, Curtis Hughes, and Nicole Murphy. Recent seasons have also featured works by Julius Eastman, Sam Pluta, Jessie Cox, Philippe Hurel, Meshuggah, Katherine Young, Louis Andriessen, Chaya Czernowin, Klaus Lang, Björk, and more.

The Hinge Quartet’s educational initiatives have included residencies and workshops throughout the United States at institutions such as the Cincinnati University College-Conservatory of Music, Boston Conservatory at Berklee, UC Berkeley, East Carolina University, Ohio University, Miami University, the University of Georgia, St. Cloud State University, the University of Montana, and Western Michigan University. In 2019-20 the Hinge Quartet partnered with UMass Lowell in an innovative mentorship program in which the ensemble worked closely with an undergraduate performer throughout the season.

Ham radio, formally amateur radio, is two-way radio communication by licensed hobbyists on frequency bands set aside for them. Operators talk by voice, send Morse code, or pass text, images and data through a computer, across town, across the world, through satellites, and to the International Space Station.
What is Ham Radio? · ARRL is the overview from the national association for amateur radio in the United States.

Amateurs were building and operating radio stations in the first decades of the twentieth century, soon after radio itself. The ARRL was founded in 1914 to relay messages between amateur stations across distances no single station could reach.
The origin of the word "ham" is uncertain. A common account is that professional telegraphers used it as an insult for clumsy operators, and amateurs later adopted it with pride.
A license to transmit. In the United States, an operator must pass an FCC examination before transmitting on the amateur bands. The entry-level license is the Technician class.
Listening needs no license. A receiver, including a shortwave set built from a kit, can pull in distant stations without any license. Listening of this kind is called shortwave listening.
No business. Amateur bands are for personal, non-commercial communication.

On the shortwave (HF) bands, signals bounce between the ionosphere and the ground in hops, so a modest station can reach the other side of the planet. How far a band reaches changes with the time of day, the season, and the sunspot cycle.
A good ground connection improves a simple receiver: driving a metal rod into the earth gives the antenna circuit a return path.
Emergency communication: when regular networks failed after the 9/11 attacks and during Hurricane Katrina, amateur operators carried messages for public service agencies.
Contacting the International Space Station, bouncing signals off the moon, and working amateur satellites.
